quote: Yes. Our son our daughter and son.
stewart_read: Frederick discloses adult children on the title, but the rep says only 'Okay. Awesome' and moves to the next verify item without asking whether the son or daughter should be included in the appointment or credit-qualified separately.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may be deferring co-owner scheduling until day-of since the wife (not the children) ends up joining the booking call, suggesting the children may be silent co-owners not involved in day-to-day decisions.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to ask a quick follow-up — 'are they involved in this decision, or is it just you and your wife?' — to resolve who actually needs to be on the appointment, per protocols.adult_child_decision_maker.

quote: No. I've been interested for a long time. Prices are coming down, and some of the offsets being offered by the state are attractive.
stewart_read: This is a specific, personalizable interest reason (price trend + state incentives) that could anchor both the pitch and the text follow-up tieback, but the rep only reflects it back generically ('just kinda looking into it now for the the programs and just the extra benefits') and never returns to it.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to hold onto specific interest language like 'state offsets' and use it explicitly in the close or text follow-up tieback rather than paraphrasing it into a generic category.

quote: Well, it's classic asphalt shingles, but it's not a classic roof.
stewart_read: Customer volunteers detail about roof shape suggesting easy install, and the rep responds warmly and accurately ('you're getting, you know, more sun throughout the day, not having to worry about the steep pitches'), which is a good micro-affirmation of a positive install signal.
coaching_implication: This is a moment to credit — rep engaged with unsolicited detail naturally rather than rushing past it. Reinforce this instinct as a model for other verify-section moments.

quote: Probably around 3,000 k w a year.
stewart_read: Customer self-reports high dual-200-amp-panel usage and a bill ranging $300-$620, but the rep's only response is a flat math confirmation ('I'll just do the math there. So 3,000 times 12 will tell us kind of your annual usage') with no emotional reflection of the pain represented by that range.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to verbally acknowledge the bill swing ('that's a big range to deal with every month') before pivoting to the math, converting the number into leverage rather than just a data input.

quote: We we consume a lot of electricity.
stewart_read: Customer directly states high consumption tied to dual 200-amp service — a strong qualifying signal for a larger system — but the rep's response ('Yeah. Okay. Gotcha. Sounds good.') does not acknowledge or amplify it.
coaching_implication: High-usage disclosures like this are exactly what should be flipped into anticipation for the appointment ('that's great context for our design team to build a system that actually covers it') rather than passed over with a filler acknowledgment.

quote: I would suggest just writing down any questions or, you know, maybe some concerns you might have about solar just so when our specialist is over, you know, obviously, we don't wanna miss any information you're looking for.
stewart_read: This is a proactive, forward-looking move that primes the customer to engage seriously before the closer call, beyond the standard button-up script requirements.
coaching_implication: This is a strong technique worth reinforcing across the floor — credit the rep for this addition to the standard button-up and encourage consistent use.
